lesson.title: Wi Fi Roaming: Handoff Without a Carrier Running the Show
lesson.summary: Wi Fi roaming lets a client move between access points sharing the same network name, deciding for itself when to reassociate, with extensions like 802.11k, 802.11v, and 802.11r shrinking the gap that a fresh handshake would otherwise cause.
lesson.body:
Wi Fi roaming is what happens when a laptop or phone walks from the coverage area of one access point to another without losing its network connection, and it is essentially the same problem handoff solves in a cellular network, just without a mobile carrier orchestrating the transition from a central core. Multiple access points sharing the same SSID form what the 802.11 standard calls an extended service set, and roaming is the client device's job of picking the best access point in that set and reassociating with it as signal conditions change.

Unlike a cellular handoff, which the network largely controls, classic Wi Fi roaming decisions are made by the client device itself. The device continuously measures the received signal strength indicator (RSSI) of its current access point, and when that signal drops below a threshold set by the device's own driver, it scans for other access points advertising the same SSID and reassociates with whichever one looks strongest. Because the device tears down its old association before completing the new one, ordinary Wi Fi roaming is a break before make process, and every reassociation on a WPA2 or WPA3 network normally requires a fresh authentication handshake, which introduces a delay of anywhere from tens of milliseconds to a few seconds.

That delay is tolerable for web browsing but disruptive for a voice or video call, so the 802.11 standard added extensions specifically to shrink it. 802.11k lets an access point hand a client a neighbor report listing nearby access points and their channels, so the device does not have to scan blindly. 802.11v adds BSS transition management, letting the network suggest that a client move to a specific access point before its current signal degrades too far. 802.11r, commonly marketed as fast BSS transition or fast roaming, lets a device pre negotiate encryption keys with a target access point before it disconnects from the current one, cutting the reauthentication delay down to roughly the time it takes to swap channels.

Not every client roams well even with these extensions available, since the decision of when to leave the current access point is still made locally on the device, using thresholds a manufacturer's driver chooses. A device that waits too long to roam becomes what network administrators call a sticky client, clinging to a weak, distant access point long after a much stronger one is available nearby, which drags down its own throughput and, on a busy network, can waste airtime that other devices need.

Because all of the access points in a roaming domain sit behind the same wired network and typically share one IP subnet, a Wi Fi client keeps the same IPv4 address throughout a roam, which is what makes the transition invisible to an application above the network layer; only the radio association changes, not the address itself. This is a meaningfully different situation from cellular handoff between towers operated by the same carrier's packet core, and it is different again from Mobile IP, which exists specifically for the case where a device does change its point of attachment, and therefore its reachable address, as it moves.
